UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                      BEFORE THE
                        FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

El Paso Natural Gas Company, L.L.C.                 )                      Docket No. CP26-558-000

                        MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER, ANSWER, AND
                               MOTION TO DISMISS PROTEST

          Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”)1 and section 157.205(g) of the

Commission’s regulations,2 El Paso Natural Gas Company, L.L.C. (“EPNG”) hereby moves for

leave to answer, answers, and moves to dismiss the (i) Joint Protest and Motion to Intervene of

Sierra Club and Food & Water Watch (together, “Petitioners”) filed in this docket on October 5,

2026 (“Protest”),3 and (ii) Comments of Sierra Club and its members (“Comments”).4 The Protest

consists of generalized objections to the development of natural gas and data center infrastructure

in El Paso County, Texas, which Petitioners attempt to dress up in legal language to demand a

comprehensive and time-consuming environmental impact statement (“EIS”) to evaluate potential

impacts that have already been examined or impacts from other projects that are clearly outside

the scope of the Commission’s obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act

(“NEPA”). This demand for ever-expanding NEPA reviews is exactly the approach the Supreme

Court rejected in Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, 605 U.S. 168 (2025).

The Comments merely set forth generic objections to the development of any energy or industrial

          Because the Protest and Comments fail to identify any substantive issue with the McCloud

Lateral Project (the “Project”),6 the Commission should not treat either the Protest or Comments

as a “protest” within the meaning of section 157.205(e) of the Commission’s regulations.7 The

Commission should not mistake the Protest’s length and extensive reliance on block quotations

from caselaw as a substantive and Project-specific protest to EPNG’s Request. Accordingly,

EPNG requests that the Director of the Office of Energy Projects dismiss both the Protest and

Comments pursuant to section 157.205(g).8 Should the Commission decide to treat either the

Protest or Comments as a protest, EPNG respectfully requests the Commission waive the 30-day

reconciliation period and immediately issue an order authorizing the Project.

          Anything other than a prompt dismissal of the Protest and Comments would thwart the

purpose of the Commission’s blanket certificate program. The Commission has repeatedly

recognized that the notice and protest provisions of Subpart F of Part 157 of the Commission’s

Regulations are “streamlined procedures intended to increase flexibility and reduce regulatory and

administrative burdens,”9 and are “not intended as a vehicle to delay the resolution of matters . . .

that lack substantive basis and thus are without merit on their face.”10 Failure to dismiss the Protest

and Comments will sanction unreasonable delays for non-controversial construction projects

proceeding into an extended certificate application process under Natural Gas Act (“NGA”)

section 7 simply by filing a protest invoking “cumulative effects,” “environmental justice,” and

“segmentation” theories wholly untethered from case-specific facts about the project at issue. The

Commission should not sanction this attempted abuse of the Commission’s blanket certificate

program.           Accordingly, EPNG respectfully urges the Commission to proceed by promptly

authorizing the McCloud Lateral Project, so that EPNG may serve a creditworthy regulated utility

shipper that has, through a binding open season, procured firm transportation capacity to meet new

load in El Paso County, Texas.

     I.    BACKGROUND

           In the Request, EPNG filed a request for prior notice authorization to construct, install,

operate and maintain an approximately 5.8-mile, 16-inch outside diameter pipeline lateral and a

new delivery meter station, located in El Paso County, Texas, with a 120-foot permanent access

road segment in Otero County, New Mexico, designed to provide up to 167,000 Dth/d of firm

transportation capacity from EPNG’s South Mainline System to the new McCloud Delivery

Point.11 In connection with this Project, EPNG held a binding open season from March 16, 2026

to March 30, 2026, which resulted in a firm transportation service agreement with the Project’s

customer—El Paso Electric Company (“EPEC”), a regulated electric utility—for 100% of the

Project’s capacity.12 The open season process thus resulted in a firm service agreement with an

unaffiliated and creditworthy regulated utility shipper, which established market need for the

Project.

            The Request was submitted in compliance with the Commission’s blanket certificate

program, which is set forth, as relevant here, in sections 157.205, 157.208, 157.210, and 157.211

of the Commission’s regulations. EPNG submitted the Request pursuant to its own blanket

certificate authority issued in Docket No. CP82-435-000.13 The Request explained that the

estimated cost for the Project is $20.3 million,14 which is well below the applicable $61,650,000

cost limit for prior notice that has been established by the Commission.15

           The Request also included the environmental information required by the Commission’s

blanket certificate rules under Part 157 of the Commission’s regulations, including an

environmental report that contains an analysis of the potential environmental impacts associated

with the Project (the “Environmental Report”).16 The Request explained that a total of 71.63 acres

of land will be utilized during construction, most of which would have only a temporary

construction impact. In key part, the Environmental Report explained that there would be no

expected impacts on wetlands and no expected impacts to sensitive environmental areas.17

Moreover, EPNG consulted with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the Texas Historical

Commission, and the New Mexico State Historic Preservation Office, each of which reached a “no

effect” determination with respect to listed species, critical habitat, and historic properties, as

relevant to each consulting agency.18 Ultimately, the Environmental Report supported EPNG’s

environment, or affected landowners.         On October 5, 2026, Commission staff issued an

Environmental Assessment Report (“EA”) for the Project, concluding that “approval of the

proposed Project . . . would not constitute a major federal action significantly affecting the quality

of the human environment.”19

 II.      ANSWER

          Neither the Protest nor the Comments raise any substantive issues warranting case-specific

review under NGA section 7. The Protest advances five categories of argument: (i) that FERC

must prepare an EIS and conduct a free-standing cumulative-effects analysis of the Project together

with a proposed downstream power generation facility, a proposed data center, the Desert

Southwest Pipeline, the Newman Power Station, and the Borderlands Expressway; (ii) that the

Project will have disproportionate environmental justice impacts on the community of Chaparral,

New Mexico, and thus the Commission must include an environmental justice analysis in its NEPA

review; (iii) that the Project is impermissibly segmented from the downstream power plant and

data center and thus the NEPA review should consider all three projects in the demanded EIS; (iv)

that EPNG’s blanket certificate, which was issued in 1982, no longer provides an adequate basis

for authorizing the Project in light of changes in the environmental baseline; and (v) that the Project

is contrary to the public convenience and necessity under section 7 of the NGA.20 Each argument

is either foreclosed by recent and dispositive Commission and court precedent or is inapposite to

the facts of this specific Project. None rises to the level of a substantive, project-specific objection

that justifies converting EPNG’s request into a case-specific proceeding under NGA section 7.

            A.          Additional Analysis of Cumulative Effects Is Unwarranted

           Petitioners claim that the Project would have significant cumulative effects when combined

with other past, present, and reasonably foreseeable projects, and thus demand that FERC Staff

prepare an EIS for the Project to assess these effects.21 At the outset, however, some context is

needed. EPNG’s McCloud Lateral Project consists of a 5.8-mile, 16-inch outside diameter

pipeline lateral off the EPNG mainline.22 The lateral would require only 26 acres of permanent

land use across open shrub-scrub land, cross two ephemeral washes (and no other waterbodies),

and utilize two horizontal directional drills to cross highways.23 The Project would have no

significant effects on wildlife, endangered or threatened species, or impact historic properties.24

The Project involves no compression, with the only operational emissions being extremely minor

fugitive emissions, meaning the Project would have no significant impacts on air quality.25 The

construction timeline for the Project is only three months.26 Such a project does not merit an EIS.27

           With its decision in Eastern Gas Transmission and Storage, Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,218

(2026), the Commission explained that NEPA contains no reference to cumulative effects, and

with the withdrawal of the CEQ regulations, the “procedural exercise” of identifying a distinct and

separate category of cumulative effects “has proven to ultimately disserve NEPA’s goal of

supporting environmentally informed decision making without imposing undue procedural

in a NEPA document, where the details that need to be included are a factual determination for the

agency; and courts must defer to an agency’s discretionary decisions about “whether to analyze

Commission’s determinations on the scope and detail of its analysis of other reasonably

foreseeable projects that may affect the same resources as the proposed action.

          Petitioners’ reliance on Healthy Gulf v. FERC, 107 F.4th 1033 (D.C. Cir. 2024) is

unwarranted, and since Healthy Gulf was decided before Seven County and Eastern Gas, it

therefore must be read in light of them. Moreover, Healthy Gulf is not the end of the story. In

response to the same cumulative impacts arguments raised in Healthy Gulf, the D.C. Circuit in

Better Bayou subsequently upheld a cumulative impacts analysis that relied on the same threshold

for concluding impacts would be insignificant where the Commission explained how the use of

this threshold was consistent with a proper cumulative effects analysis.40 In any event, Healthy

Gulf faulted the Commission for assuming insignificant incremental effects necessarily produce

insignificant cumulative effects; here, EPNG does not rely on such an inference. The record

contains project-specific environmental findings (acreage, species, historic properties, sensitive

areas) that stand on their own.

            B.     The Commission Need Not Prepare a Specific Environmental Justice Analysis

           Petitioners claim that EPNG failed to consider environmental justice impacts to the

community of Chaparral, New Mexico.41 Petitioners’ arguments are misplaced for several reasons.

As an initial matter, Petitioners misunderstand the Commission’s approach to considering potential

impacts to nearby communities. As directed by the Presidential Executive Order 14154, the

Commission is no longer required to conduct a separate environmental justice analysis.42 Rather,

the Commission takes a holistic approach, “consider[ing] impacts to all potentially affected

communities”43 of the project at hand. EPNG’s Environmental Report provides information

pertaining to potential impacts from the project including land use, visual resources,

socioeconomics, and air quality and noise impacts.44 As detailed in the Environmental Report,

only minimal impacts are anticipated given the “short-term and temporary nature of construction-

related activities,”45 the “measures to avoid and minimize environmental impacts,”46 and because

“[c]onstruction impacts will be confined to the 75-foot-wide corridor” which includes 45 feet of

            Finally, while Petitioners claim the Project “lies in the direct area of the proposed pipeline

route,”52 EPNG notes that none of the proposed pipeline will be located within New Mexico. A

short portion of the proposed Lateral will run parallel to the Chaparral County border, but the

pipeline lateral will be located in El Paso County, Texas, as the Lateral will start approximately 2

miles south of the New Mexico border and terminate south of the Otero, New Mexico border.

           C.        The Segmentation Argument Fails Because FERC Lacks Jurisdiction Over the
                     Downstream Power Plant and Data Center

           Petitioners next assert that the McCloud Lateral Project, the generation facility to be served

by the Project, and the Meta El Paso data center must be reviewed in the same EIS as connected

actions.53 But Petitioners ignore Supreme Court and D.C. Circuit precedent: “In sum, after Seven

County, agencies are no longer ‘required to analyze the effects of projects over which they do not

exercise regulatory authority.’”54 Here, FERC’s jurisdiction under section 7 of the NGA extends

only to interstate natural gas transportation facilities. The downstream power plant, however, is a

state-regulated generation facility, and the data center is a private commercial facility. Neither is

subject to the Commission’s jurisdiction or is part of the Commission’s proposed agency action.55

Thus, Petitioners “demand exactly what Seven County says we cannot demand,”56 as NEPA does

not require an agency to “analyze the effects of projects over which [it does] not exercise regulatory

authority.”57 Moreover, the D.C. Circuit has already rejected a similar connected action argument

           D.    EPNG’s Blanket Certificate Authority Remains Valid and in Full Force and
                 Effect

           The Protest asserts that it would be “inappropriate” to authorize the Project under EPNG’s

blanket certificate authority on the sole basis that EPNG’s initial certificate was issued over four

decades ago.59 The Protest cites to no legal precedent or authority to support this position, and it

amounts to a frivolous challenge to EPNG’s blanket certificate authority as well as to the

Commission’s blanket certificate program.

           A plain reading of the Commission’s regulations forecloses the Protest’s position: “A

blanket certificate issued pursuant to this subpart authorizes the certificate holder, in accordance

with the provisions of this subpart, to engage in any of the activities specified in § 157.208 through

§ 157.218 (as may be amended from time to time).”60 Nothing in this regulation establishes a

sunset date for a certificate holder’s blanket certificate authorization. Nor does the Commission’s

by the Commission. Of course, the Protest does not allege that EPNG’s blanket certificate

exercise this blanket certificate authority in a manner consistent with the Commission’s

holders with blanket certificate authority that was issued four decades ago or longer, including for

blanket certificate projects undertaken by EPNG itself.62

          E.    EPNG Has Demonstrated Market Need through a Firm Service Agreement for
                100% of the Project’s Capacity

          EPNG has established clear marked need for the Project as evidenced by a binding firm

service agreement with a customer that has subscribed to 100% of the Project capacity. It remains

the Commission’s policy that “precedent agreements are the best evidence” of project need and

the same applies to transportation service agreements.63 In fact, the Commission “will not look

Moreover, in the specific context of prior notice requests, the Commission routinely finds strong

evidence of project need where 100% of the project’s capacity has been subscribed pursuant to the

terms of a binding customer agreement—even where that agreement is only with one customer

(which is common in the prior notice context, due to the inherently limited nature of the types of
